extracted.intended_audience: aspiring screenwriters, film students, and general readers researching Blake Snyder's Save the Cat! method
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and criteria for structuring mainstream feature films using Blake Snyder's Save the Cat approach, including logline rules, Snyder's story-type categories, a detailed beat sheet with page targets, planning techniques (The Board), and a set of screenwriting

rubrics_metrics.name: Logline requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: A logline is a one- or two-sentence summary that encapsulates tone, potential, dilemma, characters, and audience; Snyder argues it should be developed prior to writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The ideal logline must satisfy four requirements: Irony — be ironic and emotionally involving; A compelling mental picture — imply the entire movie; Audience and cost — demarcate target audience and potential production cost; A killer title — include a title that cleverly communicates the story's substance. Snyder links this to the idea of high-concept and recommends testing loglines by pitching them aloud and revising.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Snyder's story-type categories
rubrics_metrics.description: Snyder recommends categorizing movies by story type rather than traditional genre labels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Categories include: Monster in the House (e.g., Jaws, Alien), Golden Fleece (Star Wars, Wizard of Oz), Out of the Bottle (Groundhog Day), Dude with a Problem (Die Hard), Rites of Passage, Buddy Love, Whydunit, The Fool Triumphant, Institutionalized, Superhero, etc. Screen similar films and analyze strengths/weaknesses within the same category.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hero selection /character criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose a hero who is best suited to carry the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The ideal hero experiences the most conflict in the story's situation, has the longest emotional journey, and pursues a primal goal (survival, hunger, sex, protecting loved ones).

rubrics_metrics.name: Three-act structure mapping (thesis/antithesis/synthesis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Snyder's overall structure follows a classic three-act model but mapped to specific beats and page counts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each act corresponds to thesis (Act I), antithesis (Act II), and synthesis (Act III); Snyder's Beat Sheet specifies beats and approximate page numbers to allocate story events across the three acts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opening Image (p. 1)
rubrics_metrics.description: The first visual of the movie that establishes tone, mood, type, and scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Should give an immediate impression of what kind of movie it is; sets the baseline to be contrasted with the Final Image.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theme Stated (p. 5)
rubrics_metrics.description: A secondary character states the theme of the movie, usually in an offhand way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This early line or moment hints at the thematic throughline that the story will explore; it should be subtle rather than didactic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Set-up (p. 1–10)
rubrics_metrics.description: The first ten pages showing the hero's world before the inciting change; introduces or hints at all major A-story characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present the 'Six Things That Need Fixing' — missing elements in the hero's life (character flaws, needs, wishes). Snyder notes six is arbitrary but suggests these items establish what must change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Catalyst (p. 12)
rubrics_metrics.description: A life-changing moment that presents the journey to the hero or makes staying in stasis impossible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also called the Inciting Incident or Call to Adventure; should be a clear event that propels the narrative into motion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Debate (p. 12–25)
rubrics_metrics.description: The section where the hero debates what to do about the Catalyst, may initially refuse then accept the challenge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shows the hero's internal conflict and stakes before committing to Act II; useful for character development and clarifying the cost of action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Break into Two (p. 25)
rubrics_metrics.description: The hero makes the choice to go on the adventure, propelling the story into Act II.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This choice should feel consequential and move the protagonist from the old world into the new 'promise of the premise' territory.

rubrics_metrics.name: B Story (p. 30)
rubrics_metrics.description: A subplot that provides a thematic counterpoint and a breather from the A story, often a love story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carries the theme in a different scope and often helps the protagonist grow; new characters may be introduced here. Snyder argues its role is to give the audience a breather after Break into Two.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fun and Games (p. 30–55)
rubrics_metrics.description: First half of Act Two that delivers 'the promise of the premise' — the core enjoyable sequences of the concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Often lighter in tone and focused on the idea that sold the concept; not primarily about forward plot escalation but about delivering the movie's hook.

rubrics_metrics.name: Midpoint (p. 55)
rubrics_metrics.description: A turning point that is either a false victory or a false defeat and raises the stakes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Often corresponds oppositely to the All Is Lost beat (e.g., if Midpoint is false defeat, All Is Lost may be false victory); should shift tone and escalation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bad Guys Close In (p. 55–75)
rubrics_metrics.description: Obstacles mount and antagonistic forces regroup; things get worse for the hero.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complicates the hero's progress with increasing, seemingly insurmountable problems that make the eventual collapse believable.

rubrics_metrics.name: All Is Lost (p. 75)
rubrics_metrics.description: The story's lowest beat where the hero's life falls apart and there appears to be no hope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Often includes a 'whiff of death' (literal or metaphorical) such as hinted suicide or death of a mentor; should feel like a genuine nadir.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dark Night of the Soul (p. 75–85)
rubrics_metrics.description: The period of despair immediately after All Is Lost when the hero wallows before finding resolve.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emotional low point before the hero digs deep and discovers the means to move forward; sets up the Break into Three.

rubrics_metrics.name: Break into Three (p. 85)
rubrics_metrics.description: A and B stories intertwine and help the hero find a solution; the final act begins.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This beat marks the protagonist applying lessons learned and choosing a new, usually active approach to the remaining conflict.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finale (p. 85–110)
rubrics_metrics.description: Resolution where the hero applies lessons, the old world is turned over and a new world is created; antagonists are dealt with in ascending order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Snyder emphasizes it's not enough for the hero to merely succeed; they must change the world. Structure the finale so lesser threats are resolved first, building to the biggest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Final Image (p. 110)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mirrors the Opening Image to show that change has occurred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides emotional closure by contrasting with the opening moment and demonstrating the hero's transformation.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Board (index-card planning)
rubrics_metrics.description: A visual planning method using a cork board divided into four rows (Act One, first half of Act Two, second half of Act Two, Act Three) with index cards for scenes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create an index card for each scene including emotional change and conflict; color-code cards by characters, storylines, and themes to visualize structure and pacing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Immutable laws and screenwriting tricks
rubrics_metrics.description: Collected rules and tricks Snyder recommends for crafting and fixing screenplays.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes the titular 'Save the Cat' rule (hero must do something that makes the audience like them and want them to win — e.g., Aladdin shares stolen food), the 'Pope in the Pool' (introducing exposition without boring the audience), and other practical heuristics for pacing, tone, and audience sympathy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Script troubleshooting / identifying weak points
rubrics_metrics.description: Methods for diagnosing flaws in a finished script and ways to fix them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Snyder offers approaches to spot structural, character, or pacing weaknesses and prescribes fixes often by rebalancing beats, clarifying stakes, or adjusting character arcs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategies for selling a script
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical advice for marketing scripts and navigating the film industry to get a script produced or noticed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Final chapter discusses tactics for pitching, networking, and positioning a screenplay for sale; ties back to logline/high-concept and marketability considerations (audience and cost).
